name: Sex-positive feminism
summary: Sex-positive feminism holds that sexual freedom is essential to women's freedom and opposes legal and social controls on consensual adult sexual activity, whether they come from the state, religious conservatives or other feminists. It rejects the claim that pornography and sex work are inherently degrading, supports decriminalising sex work, and defends sexual minorities, treating consent as the central test. It emerged from the 1980s feminist sex wars as a response to the anti-pornography feminism of Andrea Dworkin and Catharine MacKinnon.
scope: The pro-sex or sex-radical strand of US-centred second- and third-wave feminism from about 1979 onward: Ellen Willis, Gayle Rubin (Thinking Sex, 1984), Carole Vance and the Barnard conference, the Feminist Anti-Censorship Task Force, Nadine Strossen, and later writers such as Carol Queen. It does not cover feminism generally or sexual-liberation movements that were not feminist. Because it is a movement about sexuality, most economic, foreign-policy and constitutional statements are unaddressed and are answered at low confidence.

keyFigures.name: Gayle Rubin
keyFigures.role: Author of the 1984 essay Thinking Sex, a founding text of sex-radical feminism.

keyFigures.name: Ellen Willis
keyFigures.role: Critic of anti-pornography feminism, credited with coining 'pro-sex feminism' and founder of FACT.

keyFigures.name: Nadine Strossen
keyFigures.role: Author of Defending Pornography and a founder of Feminists for Free Expression.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Adherents defend commercial sex markets as legitimate work (s2) but are not committed to a general market-versus-state view, so this is split.

worker-ownership.rationale: Neither the sources nor adherents' writings take a position on worker ownership; sex-work-as-work advocates (s2) are split on economic models.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Sex-positive feminists want the state out of private sexual life (s1), which makes broad surveillance unattractive, though terrorism is never discussed.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Strossen, a leading voice, argues against censorship and for answering speech with speech (s4), but hate speech laws are not a central issue for the movement.

state-harmful.rationale: Adherents favour minimal state involvement in sexuality (s1) but still look to courts and law for protection of rights, so they are not anti-statist overall.

empower-police-military.rationale: Moved (statement review, 2026-11-11) to police-more-powers: its rationale is about police powers, and this statement now asks only about military spending.

reviewHistory.rationale: Adherents campaign against policing of sex workers and sexual minorities (s2, s6), so more police authority is mildly opposed.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Moved (statement review, 2026-11-11) to police-more-powers: its rationale is about police powers, and this statement now asks only about military spending.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: The World Charter for Prostitutes' Rights demanded decriminalisation of all adult prostitution and sex-positive feminists support decriminalisation where it is illegal (s2, s1).

traditional-family.rationale: Rubin's charmed circle ranks married, procreative, monogamous sex as privileged and criticises treating it as the only legitimate form (s6).

abortion-legal.rationale: Rubin cites abortion access among the constraints on sexually active women (s1), and the movement descends from contraception reformers such as Margaret Sanger.

more-religion-public.rationale: The movement criticises Christian sexual morality and conservative uses of marriage doctrine to restrict women (s1).

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Sex-positive scholars highlight Black women's agency in porn (s2), but remedying historical racial injustice is not a topic the sources address.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Rubin rejects sexual essentialism and holds gender and orientation are socially shaped; adherents support gender self-determination (s1).

gradual-change.rationale: Adherents challenge established sexual norms and institutions rather than defer to them (s6), though they do not call for revolution.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The sources are silent; the movement embraces technologies like online and feminist porn but has no general techno-optimism.

one-party-rule.rationale: Sex-positive feminism defends diversity of sexual expression against enforced orthodoxy (s5), which is incompatible with party-imposed ideology.

direct-votes.rationale: FACT fought local ordinances passed by legislatures and wary of moral majorities, so rule by popular vote on sexual matters is a danger they perceive.

separate-church-state.rationale: Sex-positive feminists criticise religiously rooted limits on sex and law reflecting Christian morality (s1), which supports separation.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The movement opposes laws built on religious sexual morality, such as limiting sex to marriage (s1).

colonial-reparations.rationale: Reparations for colonialism are absent from the sources, and adherents' views vary across the left and liberal spectrum.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The movement defends individual sexual autonomy against community moral demands (s1, s6).

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Environmental ethics is unconnected to the movement's literature; its constructionism (s6) says little about nature's value.

restore-past-order.rationale: The movement is explicitly against the sexual order that treats some acts as natural and others as bad (s6), so restoring a lost order is opposed.

direct-action.rationale: Some groups (Samois, COYOTE) used activism but FACT worked through courts and legislative testimony, so adherents are split.

means-match-ends.rationale: FACT's litigation and testimony (s5) were conventional means, but no stated doctrine ties methods to ends.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about imperialism, and the statement now asks only whether capitalism inevitably causes wars between great powers.

reviewHistory.rationale: Theories of imperialism are not part of this movement's writing; left and liberal adherents would differ.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about imperialism, and the statement now asks only whether capitalism inevitably causes wars between great powers.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

taxation-theft.rationale: Adherents favour minimal state involvement in sexuality (s1), not in taxation; some libertarian-feminist voices (McElroy, s3) differ, so mild disagreement.

harm-principle.rationale: Ann Ferguson states that consent should be the only restriction on sexual activity, and the movement opposes controls on consensual adult sex (s1).

individual-rights-only.rationale: Rubin sees rights of sexual minorities as group-based, while liberal adherents focus on individuals; split.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Rubin's anti-essentialism (s6) opposes biological explanations of social hierarchy; race is not specifically addressed.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Expansionism conflicts with the movement's general anti-authoritarian, cosmopolitan stance, though it is never discussed.

bound-labor.rationale: The movement's core demand is consent and the right to exit or refuse in work (s2), the opposite of bound labour.

universal-morality.rationale: Sex-positive feminists reject a single sexual morality (s6) yet hold universal consent norms; split.

single-common-good.rationale: The movement stresses benign variation among sexual lifeways (s6), counter to one common good set by reason.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival is unrelated to sexual politics and absent from the sources.

class-collaboration.rationale: Sex-positive feminists are split between socialist and liberal economics, and the sources do not settle class relations.

dominated-front.rationale: Anti-Western bloc politics are absent from the movement's concerns.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Sex-positive feminism holds that women's liberation requires sexual freedom, rejecting legal role distinctions; its history opposes conservative sex-role doctrine (s1).

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Sex-radical feminists distrust the patriarchy and law to protect women, and Rubin blames family, religion, state and psychiatry for women's oppression (s1); some stress that feminism is not the whole theory of sex (s3).

night-watchman-state.rationale: The movement wants the state out of sexuality (s1) but accepts legal protection and anti-discrimination law; a minimal state is not endorsed.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Rubin argues no one should be ranked as sexually inferior and the movement stresses equal rights for sexual minorities (s6).

consent-of-governed.rationale: Consent is the movement's central ethical concept in sex (s1), but it does not theorise political legitimacy.

population-transfer.rationale: The movement opposes persecuting disfavoured groups as such (s6); transfer of minorities is the opposite.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Consent norms resemble this but the statement's absolute property-and-force framing is libertarian; adherents are split (s3).

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: FACT opposed suppressing expression, even offensive; banning parties is not directly discussed.

separated-powers.rationale: FACT relied on courts and the First Amendment to check legislatures (s5).

vanguard-party.rationale: Vanguard authority over members is alien to the movement's pluralism (s5).

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Housing tenure policy is not within the movement's scope.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The movement values benign variation among people and lifeways (s6), which rejects this claim.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: FACT defended constitutional protections against majority and state suppression (s5), so suspending them is opposed.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Price regulation is absent from the sources and unrelated to sexual politics.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: FACT stressed variety among feminists against imposed unity (s5), so binding party discipline is mildly disfavoured.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Revolutionary defeatism is a Marxist-Leninist doctrine absent from this movement.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Strossen argues that labelling material "pornography" is used to dismiss its value and that censorship laws chill adult access to books across the political spectrum.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Alliance policy is unrelated to the movement's concerns.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: National reunification has no connection to the movement's literature.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Rubin's call for a concept of benign variation, compared to valuing other cultures without ranking them as inferior (s6), extends by analogy to cultures, though she applies it to sexuality.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: The movement treats sexuality as potentially positive and supports sexual self-knowledge; sexual education grew from reformers like Dennett and Kinsey (s1).

restrict-pornography.rationale: Sex-positive feminism holds porn is not inherently degrading and opposed the Minneapolis and Indianapolis anti-porn ordinances (s1, s5, s4).

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Rubin's call for recognising benign sexual variation against social pressure to conform (s6).

constituent-assembly.rationale: Constitution-making procedure is absent from the sources; FACT used existing constitutional law (s5).

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The movement opposes restrictions on freedom of sexual expression (s1); more broadly authoritarian trade-offs conflict with its libertarian streak.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Territorial annexation disputes are unrelated to sexual politics and absent from the sources.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Ceremonial heads of state are unrelated to the movement's concerns.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Opposition to religious authority in public life (s1) rejects sacred rulers.

character-from-environment.rationale: Rubin's anti-essentialist view that sexual identities are shaped by society (s6) supports this.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: FACT relied on constitutional limits on lawmakers and officials (s5).

space-expansion.rationale: Space policy is entirely outside this literature.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Maoist debates are absent from this movement.

ban-cartels.rationale: Competition policy is unrelated to the movement's concerns.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: FACT turned to courts to strike down legislation enacted by majorities, defending minority expression (s5).

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The movement works through legal advocacy (s5), not armed revolution.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Rejection of ranking people by social value (s6) opposes rule of the supposedly more advanced.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: FACT's legal strategy rested on the First Amendment as a constraint on legislatures (s5).

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: FACT fought unconstitutional laws in court rather than by resistance (s5), so no firm view on resisting rulers.

parliament-supreme.rationale: FACT sought judicial limits on legislatures (s5), which cuts against parliamentary supremacy.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The movement is actively political, from Barnard to court briefs (s3, s5).

party-own-road.rationale: Inter-party communist relations are unrelated to this movement.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Irredentism clashes mildly with the cosmopolitan outlook but is never discussed.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Indigenous political leadership is absent from the sources.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The movement is a defence of stigmatised minorities against panic (s6), so conspiracy claims are opposed.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Rubin treats legal marriage as part of the privileged circle (s6), but adherents also seek marriage equality; split.

informal-organisation.rationale: FACT and groups like Samois were small voluntary organisations (s3, s5), but the movement states no organisational doctrine.

religious-nation.rationale: Opposition to religious definitions of society (s1).

religion-illusion.rationale: The movement criticises Christian sexual morality (s1) but does not claim religion is an illusion.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: SEP notes poverty shapes sex work (s2); structural change claims are mixed among adherents.

holocaust-denial.rationale: The movement is a defence of stigmatised minorities against panic and persecution (s6), and a historical falsehood used against a persecuted group has no support among adherents, though anti-censorship voices such as Strossen oppose legal bans (s4).

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Sex-positive feminism holds acceptance of all sexual orientations is necessary to sexual freedom and allies with LGBT activists (s1).

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The movement opposes religious regulation of sex and law (s1), so toppling rulers for not enforcing religious law is rejected.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Sex-positive feminists support self-determination of gender and promote gender fluidity; Califia wrote on transgender issues (s1).

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Opposition to religious moral authority in law (s1).

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Strossen accepts sexual harassment as illegal discrimination (s4) though warns against overreach.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: The movement is about sexuality and the sources address no debt or IMF policy.

property-franchise.rationale: Feminism grew from the fight to extend the vote beyond propertied men, and sex-positive feminists defend marginalised groups against exclusion.

racial-franchise.rationale: The movement defends sexual minorities and equal rights; limiting voting to one racial group contradicts that.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Opposing legal controls on consensual adult relationships is central, and this includes limits on who may marry.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: The movement defends persecuted minorities, and Rubin's essay criticises moral panics that single out groups.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Nothing in the sources addresses constitutional design for divided societies.

uniformed-youth.rationale: The movement opposes state and moral control over youth and sexual conduct (s1, s5); drilled national-service movements run against its libertarian outlook.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Rubin's Thinking Sex treats sexuality as historically and socially produced (s6), though the claim about sex, not only gender, goes beyond it.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The movement opposes moralised politics and religious conservatives' framing of sex as sin (s1, s3), so a good-versus-evil politics is contrary to it.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The movement defends minorities and rejects group-based exclusion (s1, s3), so reserving economic life for a majority is contrary to it.

person-over-state.rationale: The movement makes individual consent the central test and opposes state control of consensual sexual choices.

women-distinct-values.rationale: The movement opposes essentialist claims about women's nature, which it sees behind the anti-pornography side's case in the sex wars.

smash-state-machine.rationale: The movement works through law reform, litigation and cultural argument rather than overthrowing the state, as FACT's court challenges show.

shared-human-nature.rationale: The movement treats gender and sexuality as shaped by society and challenges fixed ideas of what is natural, as in Rubin's critique of the charmed circle, so a fixed human nature is doubted.

public-service-media.rationale: Adherents favour anti-censorship, so are wary of state control of media, but not hostile to publicly funded outlets; split.

farm-price-support.rationale: Farm policy is outside the movement's concerns; adherents are split by general politics.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Equal legal rights for women are the base of feminism, which the sex-positive strand shares while arguing about sexuality.

premarital-sex.rationale: It treats sexual freedom as essential to women's freedom and opposes moral controls on consensual adult sex.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Anti-censorship feminists distrusted state-led gender programmes, yet most feminists favour such bodies; adherents split.

self-ownership.rationale: Bodily autonomy and consent are central: s1 and s2 describe the defence of adults' right to use their own bodies, including in sex work and pornography.

police-more-powers.rationale: Adherents campaign against policing of sex workers and sexual minorities (s2, s6), so more police authority is mildly opposed. (Moved from empower-police-military, 2026-11-11, when that statement became about military spending alone.)

missingStatements.text: Consensual sadomasochism and other unconventional sexual practices between adults should be accepted as legitimate.
missingStatements.rationale: Samois defended BDSM as consistent with feminism and Rubin's charmed circle criticises ranking some consensual acts as bad or unnatural.

missingStatements.text: Women's sexual pleasure should be openly affirmed rather than treated as dangerous or shameful.
missingStatements.rationale: Sex-positive feminism treats sexuality as a potentially positive force and credits Betty Dodson's championing of women's pleasure; Vance faults anti-porn feminism's shame-based attitudes.
missingStatements.declined: Affirming women's sexual pleasure is broadly accepted and would not separate ideologies.

notes: Adherents differ on marriage (marriage equality versus critique of marriage as a privileged institution), on economic questions, and on how far sex work is ordinary work. Critics such as Ariel Levy hold that popular sex positivity became 'raunch culture'; the profile follows adherents, not critics.
